Treated wood pilings that once lasted 30-plus years may run only 10 to 15 years in saltwater environments; brackish water like Hull Creek is gentler, but it still accelerates wear compared to fresh water, and Will's direct experience with these pilings is the more useful data point than any national average. writerChanges.before:
NFIP premiums in Virginia under Risk Rating 2.0 run $250 to $1,973 a year for Zone AE, with the state median around $664. Properties at or near base flood elevation (which describes most waterfront lots with dock access) tend toward the upper half of that range. Figure $900 to $1,600 as a realistic planning number for a property like this one if you don't yet have your own Elevation Certificate.

Two things buyers miss: first, flood coverage is not in your standard homeowners policy. It's a completely separate policy. You will write two checks. Second, new NFIP policies have a 30-day waiting period before they take effect, so you can't buy coverage the week before a named storm and expect it to stick.
writerChanges.after: The key fact most buyers miss: flood coverage isn't in your standard homeowners policy. It's a separate policy, a separate check. Under FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0, individual premiums are driven by elevation, foundation type, and distance to water — the flood zone tells you roughly where you sit but doesn't tell you what you'll pay. Get a quote before you make an offer, not after.
writerChanges.why: Fix #2: compressed flood insurance section. Removed NFIP range ($250–$1,973), state median ($664), planning-range filler ($900–$1,600), and the 30-day waiting-period logistics paragraph. Kept the most actionable buyer insight. Also contracted 'is not' → 'isn't', 'You will write' → removed, per Fix #4.
